Clinical Reference

Osteomyelitis

On this page
Osteomyelitis is infection of bone. Bacteria reach the bone, the host's own inflammatory response thromboses the bone's blood supply, and the resulting dead bone (sequestrum) becomes a biofilm sanctuary that antibiotics cannot reach. That one fact — dead bone does not take antibiotics — explains nearly every management decision that follows.
S. aureus — the #1 pathogen in every subtype Bone biopsy + culture = the gold standard Chronic osteo is a SURGICAL disease 6 weeks from the last debridement Oral ≈ IV (OVIVA, NEJM 2019)
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story, told so the drugs make sense

Bone is normally an extraordinarily hostile place for bacteria: it is dense, well-perfused, and patrolled. Osteomyelitis begins when that defence is breached by one of three routes — and the route you pick predicts the organism, the site, and the operation.

  • Haematogenous seeding — bacteria arrive by blood. In adults this overwhelmingly means the spine, because the vertebral end-plates are supplied by tortuous, low-flow arterioles where organisms lodge. Think bacteraemia: S. aureus, IV drug use, dialysis catheters, endocarditis.
  • Contiguous spread — infection walks in from an adjacent soft-tissue focus. The prototype is the diabetic foot ulcer: neuropathy removes protective sensation, pressure creates an ulcer, the ulcer deepens to the cortex, and the cortex is breached. Depth matters far more than diameter.
  • Direct inoculation — open fracture, surgery, gunshot, a nail through a shoe. Here the organism is whatever was on the object or the skin.

However they arrive, what happens next is the same, and it is the host who does most of the damage:

  1. Adhesion. S. aureus carries a toolkit of surface adhesins (MSCRAMMs) that grip bone collagen, fibronectin and bone sialoprotein. This is why S. aureus — and not any other organism — dominates bone infection.
  2. Inflammation. Neutrophils pour in. IL-1, TNF and RANKL activate osteoclasts, which resorb bone. The lytic destruction you eventually see on the radiograph is the patient's own osteoclasts, not the bacteria.
  3. Pressure. Pus accumulates inside a rigid, non-expandable cortex. Intramedullary pressure rises. The pus strips the periosteum off the bone and, crucially, thromboses the nutrient and periosteal vessels.
  4. Ischaemia and death. A segment of bone loses its blood supply and dies. That dead fragment is the sequestrum.
  5. Biofilm. On the avascular surface of the sequestrum (and on any hardware), bacteria build an exopolysaccharide matrix and drop into a slow-growing, metabolically dormant state. Most antibiotics kill by attacking actively dividing cells — so these bacteria become tolerant without ever becoming genetically resistant. Culture the sequestrum and the MIC looks perfectly susceptible; the drug simply cannot finish the job in situ.
  6. Chronicity. The stripped periosteum lays down a shell of new bone around the dead bone — the involucrum. Pus escapes through a hole in it (the cloaca) and tunnels out to skin as a sinus tract. Now you have chronic osteomyelitis: a relapsing infection with a built-in sanctuary.
Infected bone is a castle under siege. Systemic antibiotics are your army: they can hold the countryside and kill anything moving in perfused, living bone. But the sequestrum is a walled-off keep whose drawbridge has been destroyed — no blood vessels lead into it, so no antibiotic army can march in, no matter how long the siege lasts or how high the dose. You can besiege it for a year and the garrison will still be there. The only way to win is to tear the keep down — surgical debridement. Rifampin is the one agent that can tunnel under the wall (it penetrates biofilm and kills dormant staphylococci) — but send it in alone and the garrison learns to recognise it within days, so rifampin must always travel with a partner drug.
Pathogenesis of osteomyelitis, and the three points where therapy interrupts it. Green nodes = what your treatment actually does.

The anatomy of chronic osteomyelitis — learn these four words

Every radiology report and every orthopaedic conversation about chronic bone infection uses the same four terms. They are not trivia; each one is a direct consequence of the cascade above, and each one has a management implication.

Sequestrum, involucrum, cloaca and sinus tract — the four hallmarks of chronic osteomyelitis, and why the disease is surgical.
Sequestrum. A gross specimen of chronic osteomyelitis: a dense, dead fragment of bone lying free within an infected cavity. This is the fragment that no antibiotic can reach and that surgery must remove.
Otis Historical Archives, National Museum of Health & Medicine (OTIS Archive 1) · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Involucrum. Extracortical new bone laid down by the lifted periosteum, forming a living shell around the dead bone beneath. Its presence tells you the infection has been there for weeks to months.
Ed Uthman, Houston, TX · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Acute osteomyelitis — histology. Marrow spaces packed with neutrophils. Acute inflammation is the histological hallmark; it is the neutrophil-driven cytokine storm that activates osteoclasts and thromboses vessels.
Mikael Häggström, M.D. · CC0 / public domain · Wikimedia Commons
Chronic osteomyelitis — histology. Lymphocytes and plasma cells with fibrosis and necrotic bone replace the acute neutrophilic infiltrate. Histology from the bone biopsy is worth as much as the culture — it can be positive when culture is not.
Mikael Häggström, M.D. · CC0 / public domain · Wikimedia Commons

Why each drug class works — the through-line of this whole guide

Map each therapy onto the step it interrupts, and the treatment plan stops being a list to memorise:
  • Anti-staphylococcal β-lactams (nafcillin, oxacillin, cefazolin) — bind penicillin-binding proteins and block cell-wall cross-linking in dividing bacteria. They interrupt step 2 (the replicating population in living, perfused bone). Bactericidal, cheap, narrow — the drug of choice whenever the organism is MSSA.
  • Glycopeptides / lipopeptides / oxazolidinones (vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid) — do the same job when the organism is MRSA. Vancomycin blocks the D-Ala-D-Ala peptidoglycan precursor; daptomycin punches calcium-dependent holes in the membrane; linezolid blocks the 50S initiation complex.
  • Rifampin — inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Uniquely among these agents it is active against adherent, stationary-phase staphylococci inside biofilm, which is exactly the population the others miss. It interrupts step 5. It is also the only one that goes into the biofilm, which is why it is added specifically for retained hardware and implant infection — and why, because resistance emerges within days, it is never given alone.
  • Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) — inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV. Their real superpower in bone infection is near-complete oral bioavailability and excellent bone penetration, which is what makes oral therapy viable (and makes them rifampin's classic partner).
  • Surgical debridement — the only intervention that removes the sequestrum and the biofilm and restores a vascular bed into which antibiotics can actually be delivered. It interrupts the cascade at step 4–5, and it is why chronic osteomyelitis is fundamentally a surgical disease with an antibiotic adjunct rather than the other way round.
  • Revascularisation (in the ischaemic diabetic foot) — an antibiotic that cannot reach the bone is an antibiotic that does not work. If the foot has no blood supply, restoring it is antimicrobial therapy.
🗂️

Classification — two systems, two different jobs

Residents mix these up constantly. Lew & Waldvogel tells you how the bug got in (and therefore which bug and which workup). Cierny–Mader tells you what the surgeon has to do (and whether the patient can survive having it done).

Lew & Waldvogel — mechanism of infection

CategoryTypical patientUsual organismsWhat it changes
HaematogenousAdults: vertebral column. Also IVDU, dialysis, indwelling lines, endocarditis.S. aureus (most common), streptococci, gram-negative rods; Salmonella in sickle cell; Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Pott disease); Brucella.Blood cultures are frequently positive — draw them before antibiotics. A positive S. aureus blood culture with concordant MRI can spare the patient a biopsy. Always ask: where did the bacteraemia come from? (echo for endocarditis).
Contiguous focus (without vascular insufficiency)Post-operative, post-traumatic, open fracture, hardware, pressure ulcer, sternal wound.S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium acnes (shoulder hardware), gram-negatives; often polymicrobial.Hardware means biofilm means rifampin combination therapy ± removal. Culture the deep tissue, not the wound surface.
Contiguous with vascular insufficiencyThe diabetic foot. Also severe PAD.Frequently polymicrobial: S. aureus + streptococci + Enterobacterales ± anaerobes.Two diseases at once — infection and ischaemia. Assess perfusion (ABI, toe pressures) early; revascularisation may matter more than the antibiotic.

Cierny–Mader — the surgical staging system

Stage = anatomic type (I–IV) + physiologic host class (A/B/C). It is the system the orthopaedic surgeon is actually using when they decide how aggressive to be.

Anatomic typeWhat is infectedClassic exampleSurgical implication
I — MedullaryEndosteal / medullary cavity only.Haematogenous osteomyelitis; infected intramedullary rod.Unroofing / intramedullary reaming. Bone remains structurally stable.
II — SuperficialCortical surface only — a true contiguous infection of exposed bone.Bone at the base of a pressure or diabetic ulcer.Superficial decortication + soft-tissue coverage. The soft tissue is often the real problem.
III — LocalisedFull-thickness cortical + medullary, but a stable bone — a resectable focus.Infection after plating/internal fixation.Full-thickness debridement; bone remains stable afterwards. Dead space management needed.
IV — DiffuseCircumferential/segmental disease; the bone is unstable (or will be after debridement).Infected non-union; extensive post-traumatic osteomyelitis.Requires segmental resection plus reconstruction/stabilisation (external fixation, bone transport, flaps). The big operation.
Physiologic hostDefinitionWhat it changes
A — Normal hostNormal immune, metabolic and vascular status.Can tolerate aggressive curative surgery. Expect the best outcomes.
BL — Local compromiseLocal factors impairing healing in the affected limb: chronic lymphoedema, venous stasis, major-vessel disease, arteritis, extensive scarring, radiation fibrosis, small-vessel disease.Needs the vascular/soft-tissue problem fixed too (revascularisation, flap coverage) or the debridement will fail.
BS — Systemic compromiseSystemic factors: diabetes, malnutrition, renal or hepatic failure, chronic hypoxia, immunosuppression, malignancy, extremes of age, tobacco use.Optimise before/around surgery (glycaemia, nutrition, smoking cessation). Higher failure rate.
C — "Treatment is worse than the disease"The morbidity of curative treatment exceeds the morbidity of the infection itself, or the host cannot survive it.Do not pursue cure. Options: long-term suppressive antibiotics, simple palliative debridement, or amputation. This is an explicit, legitimate, guideline-recognised choice — not a failure.
Cierny–Mader class C is the most under-used tool on this page. An 84-year-old with dementia, a Cierny–Mader IV tibia and a class C physiology does not need a bone-transport reconstruction — they need honest goals-of-care and either suppression or an amputation that gets them walking. Naming the host class out loud on rounds is how you get that conversation started.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Osteomyelitis is a quiet disease. The single most dangerous mental error is expecting it to look like an infection — fever, leukocytosis, a sick patient. In vertebral osteomyelitis fever is absent in about half of cases; in diabetic foot osteomyelitis the white count is usually normal and the patient is usually afebrile. The findings that are reliable are the boring ones: focal pain and a raised ESR/CRP.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Focal bone pain / point tenderness over the site~80–95%The periosteum is densely innervated. Pus under pressure inside a rigid cortex stretches and strips it. The pain is deep, boring, unrelieved by rest and worse at night — which is precisely how it differs from mechanical pain.
Elevated ESR and/or CRP~90–100%IL-6 drives the hepatic acute-phase response. The most sensitive finding in the disease. A truly normal CRP makes osteomyelitis substantially less likely; a CRP that fails to fall on treatment is the earliest signal of failure.
Back or neck pain (vertebral osteomyelitis)~85–90%Infection seeds the vascular subchondral end-plate and spreads across the disc to the next vertebral body (which is why it looks nothing like a tumour, which respects the disc). Insidious, axial, often present for weeks before anyone images it.
Chronic non-healing ulcer over a bony prominence (diabetic foot)~high in that populationNeuropathy removes protective sensation → repetitive pressure → ulcer → the ulcer deepens to the cortex. An ulcer present >2 weeks, or wider/deeper than ~2 cm², or overlying bone, should be assumed to have osteomyelitis until proven otherwise.
Localised swelling, warmth, erythema~40–60%Inflammatory vasodilation, plus soft-tissue extension of pus once it breaches the cortex. Frequently absent in deep sites (spine, pelvis) where there is nothing superficial to inflame.
Fever~35–60%Cytokine-driven rise in the hypothalamic set-point. Absent in roughly half of vertebral cases and most chronic/diabetic-foot cases. An afebrile patient does not exclude bone infection — this is the trap.
Positive blood cultures (vertebral / haematogenous)~50–60%The bloodstream is often still seeded at presentation. This is exactly why you draw 2 sets before antibiotics: a positive S. aureus culture with a concordant MRI can spare the patient an invasive biopsy (IDSA 2015).
Leukocytosis~35–50%Marrow release of neutrophils. Usually normal in chronic and diabetic-foot osteomyelitis. A normal WBC is reassuring about sepsis, not about bone.
Positive probe-to-bone test (diabetic foot)Se ~87% / Sp ~83%A sterile blunt metal probe gently inserted into the ulcer strikes hard, gritty bone. If you can touch the cortex through the ulcer, the cortex is already exposed to the ulcer's flora — contiguous spread has happened. Interobserver agreement is only moderate: if you are not trained in it, do not trust your own result.
Neurologic deficit — radiculopathy, weakness, sensory level, bowel/bladder dysfunction (vertebral)~1 in 3Epidural extension of pus compresses the cord or roots; septic thrombophlebitis of the epidural venous plexus can infarct the cord outright. This is the finding that converts a ward problem into a same-night neurosurgical emergency.
Draining sinus tract / chronic drainage~15–30% (chronic)Pus takes the path of least resistance: out through the cloaca, through soft tissue, to skin. It is essentially pathognomonic of chronic osteomyelitis — and it means there is dead bone in there.
"Sausage toe" — a diffusely swollen, erythematous toe~15–20% (DFO)Osteomyelitis of a phalanx with circumferential soft-tissue inflammation. A classic and often-missed diabetic-foot tell.
Visible or palpable bone in the wound base~15–20% (DFO)Full-thickness tissue loss down to cortex. Combined with an abnormal plain film, this is close to diagnostic.
Pathological fracture<10%Osteoclast-mediated resorption plus necrosis mechanically weakens the cortex. In the spine this presents as vertebral collapse and progressive kyphosis (the gibbus of Pott disease).
Sepsis / septic shock<10%Uncommon — most osteomyelitis is indolent. When it does happen, look for an undrained abscess, a severe diabetic foot infection, or ongoing S. aureus bacteraemia with endocarditis.
Read the patternTwo questions answer most of it. (1) Is there a portal? An ulcer, a wound, hardware, an open fracture → contiguous or inoculation osteomyelitis. No portal, but a bacteraemia risk → haematogenous, and in an adult that means look at the spine. (2) Is this acute or chronic? Days-to-weeks with pain and raised markers = acute. A sinus tract, a sequestrum on film, or a story measured in months = chronic — and chronic means dead bone, which means the surgeon.
🩻

Imaging — what each test sees, when it sees it, and how good it is

The single most important imaging fact in this disease: a normal plain radiograph early on does not exclude osteomyelitis. The classic radiographic triad — osteolysis, periosteal reaction, bone destruction — is generally not evident until at least 10–20 days after symptom onset, because a substantial proportion of bone mineral has to be lost before it becomes visible on a plain film. Order the film anyway (it is cheap, it gives you a baseline, and it finds gas, foreign bodies and Charcot), but if the film is normal and your suspicion stands, either get the MRI or repeat the film in 2–3 weeks (IWGDF/IDSA 2023).

ModalityPerformance / when findings appearWhat you are looking at, and why
Plain radiograph
First test in everyone		Se ~70% · Sp ~82%
Findings lag 10–20+ days		Insensitive early because it takes substantial mineral loss to change the image. Still order it: it establishes a baseline for serial comparison, and it detects soft-tissue gas, radio-opaque foreign bodies, fractures and Charcot changes that would completely change your plan.
· Soft-tissue swelling, loss of fat planesEarliest (days)Oedema in the adjacent soft tissue — nonspecific, but the first thing to change.
· Periosteal reaction / elevation~1–2 weeksPus has stripped the periosteum, which responds by laying down new bone. The earliest bony sign.
· Focal osteopenia, loss of trabecular pattern~1–2 weeksOsteoclast-driven demineralisation. Subtle — compare to the other side.
· Cortical erosion / lytic destruction~2–3 weeks +Frank bone destruction. By the time this is obvious, the disease is established.
· Sequestrum (dense, separated dead bone)Weeks–months (chronic)Dead bone does not remodel, so it stays dense while the living bone around it demineralises — that density contrast is what makes it visible. Its presence means surgery.
· Involucrum / cloaca / bone sclerosisWeeks–months (chronic)The hallmarks of chronicity (see the pathophysiology diagram). Less commonly seen in diabetic foot osteomyelitis than in long-bone disease in younger patients.
MRI with contrast
The test of choice		Se ~95.6% · Sp ~80.7%
(diabetic foot: Se ~96.4% · Sp ~83.8%)		Low T1 marrow signal + high T2/STIR marrow oedema + post-contrast enhancement = the triad. Detects the disease within days, long before the film. Also shows what will actually change your management: epidural abscess, disc involvement, paraspinal/soft-tissue collections, and the extent of dead bone. The specificity is the weak point — Charcot, recent surgery, fracture and tumour all produce marrow oedema.
CTBest for cortex & bone detailSuperior for cortical detail, sequestrum, and gas, and it is what guides the percutaneous biopsy needle. The go-to when MRI is contraindicated (pacemaker, some hardware, severe claustrophobia).
Three-phase bone scanVery sensitive, poorly specificLights up with any increased bone turnover — fracture, surgery, tumour, Charcot. Most useful when the bone is otherwise normal and MRI cannot be done. Nearly useless in a post-operative or Charcot foot.
Labelled-WBC scintigraphy ± sulfur-colloid marrow subtraction; SPECT/CTBetter specificity than bone scanLabelled leukocytes accumulate in infection but not in the marrow-expansion of Charcot — the subtraction scan exploits exactly that. Listed by IWGDF/IDSA 2023 as an acceptable alternative to MRI.
FDG-PET/CTHigh sensitivityPerforms well in the spine and around metal (little hardware artefact). Also an IWGDF/IDSA-endorsed MRI alternative. Limited by cost and availability.
Bone biopsy + culture + histologyTHE gold standardNot imaging, but this is where the imaging pathway is supposed to end. It gives you the organism, the susceptibilities, and a histological diagnosis that can be positive even when culture is not. Everything else is a surrogate.
Osteomyelitis of the tibia. Note the aggressive permeative lytic destruction and periosteal reaction along the shaft — findings that take 2–3 weeks to appear, which is why an early film that looks normal proves nothing.
sarindam7 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Brodie abscess. A subacute, walled-off intraosseous abscess with a sclerotic rim — the bone's attempt to contain the infection. Presents as chronic focal pain with few systemic features, and is a classic mimic of a bone tumour.
Jto410 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Spondylodiscitis (L3/4), MRI + CT. The signature of vertebral osteomyelitis: end-plate destruction with loss of disc height and marrow signal change spanning the disc space in two adjacent vertebral bodies. Crossing the disc is what separates infection from malignancy — tumour respects the disc, infection eats through it.
Hellerhoff · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Spinal epidural abscess → cauda equina syndrome. The complication that must never be missed. Any patient with vertebral osteomyelitis and a new neurological deficit needs an emergent MRI of the whole spine and a neurosurgical call the same hour — not the next morning.
Jing Jing Chan & Jen Jen Oh · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Diabetic foot osteomyelitis of the 1st MTP joint. Cortical destruction and periarticular bone loss beneath a plantar ulcer. This is the most common osteomyelitis you will actually manage as an internist.
James Heilman, MD · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Pott disease. Tuberculous spondylitis with vertebral collapse and the resulting angular kyphosis (gibbus). Suspect TB when vertebral osteomyelitis is indolent over months, involves the thoracic spine, spares the disc relatively, produces large paraspinal abscesses, or occurs in a patient from a TB-endemic region or with HIV.

Lab interpretation — why each number moves, and what fools it

LabTypical move & thresholdsMechanism — why it movesWhat falsely raises / lowers it
CRP↑↑. Rises within 6–12 h; half-life ~19 h. The trend marker of choice. In diabetic foot, ESR >60 mm/h plus CRP ≥80 mg/L has a high positive predictive value for osteomyelitis (modest negative predictive value).Hepatic acute-phase protein synthesised in response to IL-6. Because it turns over in under a day, it tracks the infection almost in real time — which is precisely why it, not the ESR, is what you trend day to day.Falsely high: any inflammation — surgery, trauma, infarction, malignancy, autoimmune flare. Falsely low/normal: hepatic failure (can't make it), IL-6 blockade (tocilizumab), high-dose corticosteroids.
ESR↑↑, often markedly (>100 mm/h is common in vertebral osteo). In diabetic foot, ESR ≥70 mm/h: Se ~81%, Sp ~80%. ESR >43 mm/h plus a positive probe-to-bone correlates strongly with positive bone culture/histology.Fibrinogen and other acute-phase proteins coat red cells, reduce their surface charge and promote rouleaux, which sediment faster. It is an indirect, slow marker — it rises over days and falls over weeks.Falsely high: anaemia, pregnancy, older age, female sex, renal failure, myeloma/paraproteinaemia, obesity. Falsely low: polycythaemia, sickle cell disease (abnormal cells don't stack), extreme leukocytosis, heart failure, hypofibrinogenaemia, very high-dose steroids.
WBCOften normal — especially in chronic and diabetic-foot disease. ~35–50% have leukocytosis.Marrow release of neutrophils under G-CSF/IL-8 drive. A localised, walled-off bone infection frequently generates too little systemic cytokine signal to move it.Falsely high: corticosteroids (demargination), stress/catecholamines, smoking. Falsely low: overwhelming sepsis (consumption), marrow suppression, and — importantly — linezolid, which causes myelosuppression on prolonged therapy.
ProcalcitoninAdjunct only. For diabetic foot osteomyelitis at a cut-off of 0.33 ng/mL: Se ~85%, Sp ~67%, AUC 0.844.Released from parenchymal tissue in response to bacterial endotoxin and IL-1β/TNF; suppressed by interferon-γ (hence it stays low in viral illness).Falsely high: major surgery, trauma, burns, cardiogenic shock, renal failure. Falsely low: localised/walled-off infection with little systemic spill — which is most osteomyelitis. Never use it alone to rule out bone infection.
Blood cultures ×2Positive in ~50–60% of native vertebral osteomyelitis.Haematogenous disease means organisms are still circulating. Draw them before the first antibiotic dose — this is the single highest-yield thing you can do in the first ten minutes.A single dose of antibiotic can sterilise them. Skin contaminants (coagulase-negative staph) muddy the picture — but in a patient with hardware, that "contaminant" may be the pathogen. Repeat sets clarify.
Bone culture + histologyGold standard. Send both micro and histopathology from every specimen.Cultures give the organism and susceptibilities so you can narrow. Histology (acute or chronic inflammation, necrotic bone) can be diagnostic even when the culture is negative — for example after antibiotics have already been given.Sinus-tract and superficial wound swabs correlate poorly with the true bone pathogen and should not be used to direct therapy. Prior antibiotics reduce culture yield — which is the entire reason to hold them when the patient is stable.
HbA1cCheck in every diabetic-foot patient.Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis and oxidative burst, and glycosylates collagen — it degrades both the immune response and the healing.Falsely low with haemolysis, recent transfusion, blood loss, iron-deficiency treatment, CKD, haemoglobinopathies. Use fructosamine if the A1c is untrustworthy.
ABI / toe pressures / TcPO₂Do these in every diabetic or PAD foot. Do not skip.An antibiotic that cannot be delivered to bone cannot work. Perfusion is the rate-limiting step in whether the foot heals at all.ABI is falsely normal or high (>1.3) in diabetes and CKD because medial arterial calcification makes the vessels non-compressible — a "normal" ABI in a diabetic foot is worthless. Use toe-brachial index or TcPO₂, which the calcification does not affect.
Albumin / prealbumin↓ predicts poor healing and surgical failure.Wound healing and immune function are anabolic processes requiring substrate. Hypoalbuminaemia is also a negative acute-phase reactant, so it falls with the inflammation itself.Falls with inflammation independent of nutrition — a low albumin in acute infection reflects illness as much as malnutrition. Interpret alongside CRP.
Trend the CRP, not the ESR. CRP has a ~19-hour half-life and responds within a day; ESR takes weeks to normalise and will still be elevated at discharge in a patient who is doing perfectly well. A CRP that is flat or rising after ~4 weeks of appropriate therapy should make you suspect treatment failure and re-image (IDSA 2015). A persistently elevated ESR alone, in a patient who feels better and looks better, should not.
🦠

Microbiology — the clinical scenario tells you the organism

You will almost always have to start antibiotics before the culture is back. The way to do that intelligently is not to memorise a regimen — it is to ask "how did the bacteria get into this bone?" The route predicts the organism, and the organism dictates the drug.

Clinical scenarioExpectWhy
Any osteomyelitis, any routeStaphylococcus aureus — the most common cause in every single categoryIt is the only common pathogen equipped with a full suite of bone-matrix adhesins (MSCRAMMs) binding collagen, fibronectin and bone sialoprotein, plus the ability to form biofilm, survive intracellularly in osteoblasts, and switch to antibiotic-tolerant small-colony variants. If you remember one organism, remember this one.
Native vertebral osteomyelitisS. aureus (roughly half); streptococci; enterococci; gram-negative rods (E. coli, Proteus — think urinary source); S. lugdunensisHaematogenous seeding of the vertebral end-plate. Always hunt the source of the bacteraemia: endocarditis (get an echo if S. aureus, streptococci or enterococci), a line, a UTI, an abscess.
Indolent vertebral disease over months, thoracic spine, large paraspinal abscess, TB-endemic origin or HIVMycobacterium tuberculosis (Pott disease); Brucella (unpasteurised dairy, livestock, endemic regions); fungiSlow-growing organisms produce a slow disease. They will not grow on routine culture — you must ask the lab for AFB and fungal stains/cultures and for Brucella serology, or you will get a "no growth" and be falsely reassured.
Diabetic foot osteomyelitisFrequently polymicrobial: S. aureus + β-haemolytic streptococci + Enterobacterales ± anaerobes. In mild, previously-untreated infections in temperate climates, aerobic gram-positives alone are usually enough to cover.Contiguous spread from a chronic wound colonised by mixed skin and environmental flora. IWGDF/IDSA 2023 explicitly advises not to empirically cover Pseudomonas in temperate climates unless it has been isolated recently, or the infection is moderate/severe in a tropical/subtropical setting.
Prosthetic joint / retained hardware / post-operativeS. aureus; coagulase-negative staphylococci; Cutibacterium acnes (especially shoulder arthroplasty); gram-negatives; polymicrobialHardware is an abiotic surface with no immune surveillance — it is a biofilm scaffold. Low-virulence skin organisms that would be dismissed as contaminants anywhere else become genuine pathogens here. Cutibacterium is slow-growing: hold the cultures 10–14 days or you will miss it.
Person who injects drugsS. aureus (including MRSA); Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Candida; unusual sites — sternoclavicular joint, sacroiliac joint, pubic symphysis, vertebraeRepeated direct inoculation of skin and environmental flora straight into the bloodstream. The unusual axial sites are close to pathognomonic. Get an echocardiogram — the rate of concomitant endocarditis is high.
Puncture wound through a shoe (classic: nail through a trainer)Pseudomonas aeruginosaPseudomonas thrives in the moist foam rubber of the sole, and the nail inoculates it directly into the plantar bones. A genuinely useful piece of trivia — it changes the drug.
Sickle cell diseaseSalmonella species (classically) — but S. aureus remains common, so cover bothMicro-infarction of gut mucosa allows Salmonella translocation, while functional asplenia impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms, and infarcted bone provides the nidus. The hard clinical problem is that vaso-occlusive crisis and osteomyelitis look identical — same pain, same fever, same raised markers. MRI and cultures are what separate them.
Bite wound / human or animalPasteurella multocida (cat/dog); Eikenella corrodens (human); anaerobes; Capnocytophaga (dog, asplenic host)Direct inoculation of oral flora. Cat bites are especially prone to deep inoculation of Pasteurella because the teeth are fine and needle-like. Amoxicillin-clavulanate covers this whole set.
Immunocompromised / transplant / prolonged neutropeniaThe above plus fungi (Aspergillus, Candida), non-tuberculous mycobacteria, NocardiaImpaired cellular immunity permits organisms that never cause bone infection in an intact host. Have a low threshold for asking the lab to look for them specifically.
Staphylococcus aureus — Gram stain. Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters. The organism behind roughly half of all osteomyelitis, and the reason every empiric regimen on this page starts by covering staph.
Dr Graham Beards · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Do not treat a sinus-tract swab. Superficial swabs of a draining sinus or an ulcer surface grow the flora colonising the tract, which correlates poorly with the organism actually living in the bone. Treating the swab means you will over-treat some patients with broad-spectrum drugs they don't need and under-treat others by missing the real pathogen entirely. Culture bone, not pus from a tract.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient diagnosis, oral therapy & limb preservation
Assess

When to suspect it

🔍

The four outpatient presentations you will actually see

Osteomyelitis rarely announces itself. In clinic it hides inside four stories, and in each one the diagnosis is made by thinking of it, not by a test result landing in your inbox.

  1. The diabetic foot ulcer that will not heal. By far the most common. Any ulcer that has been open >2 weeks, is large or deep, sits over a bony prominence, shows visible or palpable bone, or is accompanied by a diffusely swollen "sausage toe" — assume osteomyelitis until you have disproved it. Do a probe-to-bone test on every one of these.
  2. New, unrelenting back pain in someone with a reason to be bacteraemic. IV drug use, haemodialysis, an indwelling line, recent S. aureus bacteraemia, recent spinal procedure, endocarditis. Axial pain, worse at night, not relieved by rest, present for weeks, ± fever (absent in half). This is native vertebral osteomyelitis and it is missed constantly — the median time from symptom onset to diagnosis is measured in weeks to months.
  3. The chronically draining wound or sinus over bone. Post-traumatic, post-surgical, over hardware, or over a pressure ulcer. A sinus tract that has been draining for months is chronic osteomyelitis; the only question is how much dead bone is under it.
  4. Pain over old hardware or a joint replacement. Persistent pain after arthroplasty — particularly early loosening or pain that never fully resolved after the operation — is prosthetic joint infection until proven otherwise. Do not let a normal white count reassure you.
Risk factorWhy it matters
Diabetes mellitus + peripheral neuropathyThe dominant risk factor worldwide. Neuropathy removes the pain that would otherwise stop the patient walking on the ulcer. Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function.
Peripheral arterial diseasePoor perfusion = poor antibiotic delivery = poor healing. Often coexists with diabetes and doubles the difficulty of everything.
Injection drug useRepeated bacteraemia; unusual axial sites; MRSA and Pseudomonas; high rate of concurrent endocarditis.
Haemodialysis / indwelling vascular accessRecurrent S. aureus bacteraemia seeding the spine.
Orthopaedic hardware / prosthetic jointA biofilm scaffold with no immune surveillance. Changes both the organism and the whole management strategy.
Recent S. aureus bacteraemiaMetastatic seeding is common. New focal bone or back pain after staph bacteraemia is osteomyelitis until imaged.
Immunosuppression, corticosteroids, malignancy, malnutritionBlunts the presentation (no fever, normal WBC) and impairs healing. Also the Cierny–Mader BS host.
Sickle cell diseaseSalmonella and S. aureus; and the diagnosis is confounded by vaso-occlusive crisis.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

The diagnostic pathway

Diagnostic algorithm for suspected osteomyelitis. The pathway is designed to end at a bone biopsy — everything before it is a surrogate.
Probe-to-bone testEvery diabetic foot ulcer, at every visit. Sterile blunt metal probe, gently advanced; positive = you feel hard, gritty bone. Se ~87%, Sp ~83% (IWGDF/IDSA 2023). Free, instant, and the single highest-yield bedside manoeuvre in this disease. Use it the way the guideline frames it: a positive test rules in osteomyelitis in a high-risk patient, and a negative test helps rule it out in a low-risk patient — so the pre-test probability is doing half the work. Caveat: interobserver agreement is only moderate — if you have not been trained in the technique, do not lean on your own negative result.Bedside
Plain radiographEveryone, first, always. Cheap, gives you a baseline for serial comparison, and finds gas, foreign bodies, fracture and Charcot. A normal film does not exclude osteomyelitis — findings lag 10–20+ days. If it is normal and suspicion persists, either go to MRI or repeat the film in 2–3 weeks (IWGDF/IDSA 2023).Initial
ESR + CRP (± procalcitonin)Everyone. Both as a diagnostic adjunct and — more importantly — as the baseline you will trend. ESR ≥70 mm/h supports DFO (Se ~81%, Sp ~80%); ESR >60 + CRP ≥80 mg/L has high PPV. IWGDF/IDSA 2023 recommends checking these when the clinical exam is equivocal. No inflammatory marker, alone, rules bone infection in or out.Initial
Blood cultures ×2Before the first antibiotic dose in anyone febrile, systemically unwell, or with suspected vertebral/haematogenous disease. Positive in ~50–60% of vertebral osteomyelitis — and a positive S. aureus, S. lugdunensis or Brucella culture with a concordant MRI means the patient can be treated without a biopsy (IDSA 2015).Before abx
MRI with contrastThe test of choice when the diagnosis remains in doubt after clinical assessment, plain films and labs (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, strong recommendation) — and in all suspected vertebral osteomyelitis (IDSA 2015, strong recommendation). Order it urgently, same-day if there is any neurological deficit. Se ~95.6% / Sp ~80.7%.If in doubt
CT / labelled-WBC SPECT / FDG-PETAlternatives when MRI is contraindicated or uninterpretable (pacemaker, hardware artefact, claustrophobia) — endorsed by IWGDF/IDSA 2023. CT is also what guides the percutaneous biopsy needle. In a Charcot foot, labelled-WBC ± marrow-subtraction scanning outperforms MRI on specificity.If MRI n/a
BONE biopsy + culture + histologyThe gold standard, and the goal of the whole pathway. Image-guided or open. IWGDF/IDSA 2023 recommends obtaining bone — not soft tissue — samples. IDSA 2015 recommends image-guided aspiration biopsy in all suspected vertebral osteomyelitis where a microbiological diagnosis has not already been established. Send both micro and histopath. Ask for AFB/fungal cultures if the course is indolent, and hold cultures 10–14 days if Cutibacterium is possible.Definitive
Vascular assessment — ABI, toe pressures, TcPO₂Every diabetic or PAD-risk foot. Perfusion determines whether the foot will heal at all. ABI is unreliable in diabetes and CKD (medial calcification makes vessels non-compressible → falsely normal or >1.3) — use toe-brachial index or TcPO₂. Refer to vascular surgery early if perfusion is poor; revascularisation may matter more than the antibiotic.DFO
HbA1c, albumin, CBC, creatinine/eGFR, LFTsGlycaemic control and nutrition drive healing; renal and hepatic function drive antibiotic dosing and monitoring choices. Get the eGFR before you pick the drug, not after.Baseline
EchocardiogramIf S. aureus, streptococcal or enterococcal bacteraemia, injection drug use, or any haematogenous osteomyelitis without an obvious source. Vertebral osteomyelitis and endocarditis travel together — finding the endocarditis changes the duration and may change the operation.If bacteraemic
Should I hold antibiotics to get the biopsy? If the patient is haemodynamically stable with a normal, stable neurological exam — yes, hold them (IDSA 2015 suggests holding empiric therapy until a microbiological diagnosis is established; holding for 1–2 weeks when feasible is reasonable). Osteomyelitis is a 6-week disease; a few days of waiting costs nothing and a culture-directed regimen is worth enormously more than a guess. If the patient is septic or has a neurological deficit — do not wait. Draw blood cultures, give antibiotics immediately, and biopsy as soon as it is feasible.
The commonest error in this disease is starting broad antibiotics in a well patient on day 1, then discovering on day 4 that you now have a negative bone culture, no organism, and a committed 6-week course of vancomycin plus cefepime that you cannot narrow. In a stable patient, the culture is worth more than the head start.

🔗

Scores we deliberately link out to rather than reimplement

These are used in osteomyelitis care but are continuous, nomogram-based or institution-weighted, and reimplementing them from memory would risk an arithmetic error at the bedside. Use the source:

  • SOFA score (organ dysfunction in sepsis) — MDCalc. Note qSOFA is reimplemented in the ICU panel of this guide, because its three criteria are exactly defined.
  • WIfI score (Wound, Ischaemia, foot Infection — limb-threat staging for the diabetic/ischaemic foot) — MDCalc. Uses the IWGDF/IDSA infection grade above as its "fI" component.
  • Charlson Comorbidity Index — MDCalc. Useful when weighing curative surgery against suppression in a Cierny–Mader class B/C host.
  • Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance — reimplemented in the Wards panel, because renal dosing of vancomycin, cefepime and levofloxacin depends on it and the formula is exact.
Treat

Outpatient management

💊

First-line → escalation

Before any of this: do not start antibiotics in a stable patient until you have a bone culture (see the decision box above), and do not treat a clinically uninfected ulcer with antibiotics at all — IWGDF/IDSA 2023 explicitly recommends against it, whether the goal is preventing infection or promoting healing. You will only select resistance.
1
Establish the diagnosis and the organism
Probe-to-bone → film → markers → MRI → bone biopsy
▾

Everything downstream is built on knowing the bug. In the clinic patient who is well, this is the step you must not skip. Get the bone culture; then narrow.

A culture-directed narrow regimen (e.g. oral flucloxacillin or a first-generation cephalosporin for MSSA) is more effective, better tolerated, cheaper and less resistance-selecting than empiric vancomycin — and osteomyelitis is a long enough course that those differences compound.
2
Fix the mechanics and the blood supply
Off-loading · debridement · revascularisation · glycaemic control
▾

Antibiotics without this fail. This is the part that most internists under-do.

  • Off-loading — total-contact cast, removable cast walker, or specialist footwear. If the patient keeps walking on the ulcer, it will not heal no matter what you prescribe.
  • Debridement — remove callus and necrotic tissue. IWGDF/IDSA 2023 suggests early surgery (within 24–48 h) combined with antibiotics for moderate and severe diabetic foot infections.
  • Revascularisation — obtain urgent joint vascular + surgical consultation in any patient with diabetes, PAD and an infected foot ulcer or gangrene (IWGDF/IDSA 2023). Restoring perfusion is antimicrobial therapy.
  • Glycaemic control and nutrition — hyperglycaemia cripples neutrophil function; hypoalbuminaemia predicts non-healing.
  • Smoking cessation — nicotine is a vasoconstrictor in a limb that has no perfusion to spare.
Prescribing antibiotics for an unoffloaded, unperfused, undebrided foot is like bailing out a boat without plugging the hole. You can bail forever and still sink.
3
Targeted antibiotics — oral where possible
OVIVA changed this: oral is non-inferior to IV
▾

The OVIVA trial (NEJM 2019, n=1054) randomised patients with bone and joint infection to oral versus IV antibiotics for the first 6 weeks and found oral therapy non-inferior (risk difference for treatment failure at 1 year −1.38%, 90% CI −4.94 to +2.19). The old dogma that bone infection mandates six weeks of IV is dead. What you need is not the intravenous route — it is a bioavailable drug, a susceptible organism, adequate source control and a reliable patient.

See the full pathogen-directed dose ladders in the Wards panel — they are identical in clinic, and most oral regimens below are what an OPAT or clinic patient will actually take home. The outpatient-friendly options:

Oral agentStartTitration / adjustmentTarget / maxWhy it worksIf allergic / intolerant

Narrow, cheap, and the most effective anti-MSSA class.Penicillin allergy (non-anaphylactic) → cephalexin 500 mg–1 g PO q6h. Severe/IgE-mediated → clindamycin, doxycycline, TMP-SMX or linezolid per susceptibilities.

Potent CYP450 inducer: it will wreck warfarin, DOACs, oral contraceptives, statins, tacrolimus, HIV protease inhibitors and methadone. What if you don't know the prior dose or the prior regimen? Don't guess and don't continue a mystery. Go back to first principles: stop, re-culture (a bone biopsy off antibiotics if the patient is stable), and restart a culture-directed regimen at the upper end of the recommended dosing range — IWGDF/IDSA 2023 explicitly advises dosing at the upper recommended range for bone infection, because bone penetration is the limiting factor.
4
Get the duration right — count from the last debridement
The most misunderstood number in this disease
▾
The treatment clock. It starts at the last debridement — not at admission, not at the first antibiotic dose.

How much bone did the surgeon leave behind? That question — not the severity of the infection — sets the duration. From IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Table 5:

SituationDurationWhy
Skin/soft-tissue infection only, mild (grade 2)1–2 weeks, oralNo bone involved. (10 days if it follows a surgical debridement.)
Skin/soft-tissue, moderate/severe (grade 3–4)2–4 weeksOral, or initially IV. Extend to 3–4 weeks if the infection is extensive, resolving slowly, or there is severe PAD.
Bone completely resected, no residual infected bone (e.g. clean-margin toe amputation)2–5 daysThere is no infected bone left. You are only treating the soft-tissue wound. Days, not weeks. This is the single most commonly over-treated scenario in medicine.
Bone resected but residual soft-tissue infection1–2 weeksTreat the soft tissue that remains.
Positive bone-margin culture/histology after resection3 weeksInfected bone was left at the margin. Supported by Gariani (CID 2021): 3 vs 6 weeks post-debridement gave comparable remission (84% vs 73%, p=0.21).
No surgery, or dead bone left in situ6 weeksThe default. Supported by Tone (Diabetes Care 2015): 6 vs 12 weeks in non-surgically-treated DFO gave similar remission (60% vs 70%) with far fewer GI adverse events (15% vs 45%, p=0.04).
Native vertebral osteomyelitis6 weeksIDSA 2015: 6 weeks of parenteral or highly bioavailable oral therapy for most patients. Bernard (Lancet 2015): 6 vs 12 weeks gave identical cure at 1 year (90.9% vs 90.8%).
Brucella vertebral osteomyelitis3 monthsIDSA 2015. Intracellular organism — needs prolonged combination therapy.
Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease)6–12 monthsStandard anti-TB regimen; duration per local TB guidance and ID input. Do not treat this like a pyogenic infection.
Prosthetic joint infection — the exception12 weeksDo NOT shorten this one. DATIPO (NEJM 2021, n=410) tested 6 vs 12 weeks in PJI managed with standard surgery: persistent infection 18.1% vs 9.4% — non-inferiority was not shown, and the short course roughly doubled the failure rate.
Longer is not safer. Tone 2015 tripled the GI adverse-event rate by going from 6 to 12 weeks and gained nothing. Every extra week of antibiotics buys C. difficile risk, line complications, cytopenias, tendinopathy and resistance — with no additional cure. Prescribe the shortest duration the evidence supports for the amount of bone that was left behind.
…except in prosthetic joint infection. Every other trial on this page pushes durations down. DATIPO (NEJM 2021) is the brake: in PJI, 6 weeks was not non-inferior to 12, and failure roughly doubled (18.1% vs 9.4%). Generalising the OVIVA/Bernard short-course message to a patient with an infected prosthesis is one of the easiest and most consequential errors in this field. PJI gets 12 weeks — and the surgical strategy (debridement with implant retention vs one- or two-stage exchange) matters more than the antibiotic anyway.
5
Refractory / not a surgical candidate
Suppression, amputation, and knowing when to stop
▾

When the infection cannot be cured — because the hardware cannot come out, the dead bone cannot be fully debrided, or the host (Cierny–Mader class C) cannot survive the operation — the goal changes from cure to control. Say this out loud; it is a legitimate plan, not a failure.

  • Chronic suppressive antibiotic therapy. A well-tolerated oral agent (commonly doxycycline, TMP-SMX, cephalexin or amoxicillin, chosen by susceptibility) continued long-term to hold the infection below the threshold of symptoms. IWGDF/IDSA 2023: suppression is warranted "generally only for individuals with retained orthopaedic hardware or extensive necrotic bone not amenable to complete debridement." Monitor CBC, renal and liver function on a defined schedule.
  • Amputation. Sometimes the fastest route back to a walking, infection-free patient. A well-healed below-knee amputation with a good prosthesis beats a limb that is salvaged after eighteen months, six operations and three readmissions. Frame it that way with the patient.
  • Palliative / comfort-focused care. In a frail, dying, or class C patient, treat pain and odour and drainage; do not chase cure.
If evidence of infection has not resolved after 4 weeks of apparently appropriate therapy, IWGDF/IDSA 2023 says to re-evaluate the patient — reconsider the diagnosis, get further imaging, re-culture, and reconsider surgery. Do not simply extend the antibiotics and hope.
Monitor

Follow-up & monitoring cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

WhatWhenWhat you are looking for / acting on
Clinical review + wound assessmentWeekly to fortnightly while on therapyPain trajectory, wound size/depth, drainage, new erythema. In DFO, is the ulcer actually closing? Is the patient off-loading?
CRPBaseline, then every 1–2 weeksShould be falling. IDSA 2015: check inflammatory markers at ~4 weeks in vertebral osteomyelitis alongside clinical assessment — unchanged or rising values at 4 weeks should raise suspicion of treatment failure.
ESRBaseline, then monthlyFalls slowly and lags weeks behind clinical improvement. A persistently high ESR in a patient who is clinically better is not treatment failure — IDSA 2015 explicitly states that persistent pain, residual neurological deficit, raised markers, or radiographic findings alone do not necessarily signify failure.
CBCWeekly if on linezolid (myelosuppression/thrombocytopenia) or prolonged β-lactam (neutropenia)Linezolid cytopenias are dose- and duration-dependent and usually reversible — but you have to be looking.
Creatinine / eGFR ± drug levelsTwice weekly on IV vancomycin; weekly on prolonged β-lactams or TMP-SMXVancomycin AKI (especially with concomitant piperacillin-tazobactam). TMP-SMX raises creatinine by blocking tubular secretion without lowering GFR — and causes real hyperkalaemia.
CK (creatine kinase)Weekly on daptomycinDaptomycin myopathy. Stop the drug if CK rises with muscle symptoms, or exceeds ~5× ULN even without symptoms.
LFTsBaseline, then every 2 weeks on rifampin, linezolid or prolonged therapyRifampin hepatotoxicity. Also warn about the harmless orange discoloration of tears, sweat and urine — and permanently stained soft contact lenses.
Repeat imagingOnly if the patient is failingIDSA 2015 advises against surgical debridement/stabilisation in patients whose bony imaging looks worse at 4–6 weeks but who are clinically improving with falling markers. Bone imaging lags healing badly. Treat the patient, not the picture.
Remission assessment (DFO)≥6 months after finishing antibioticsIWGDF/IDSA 2023 uses a minimum 6-month post-treatment follow-up to declare remission (they prefer "remission" to "cure"). Lifelong foot surveillance thereafter — these patients remain high-risk forever.
Comorbidities

How comorbidities change the disease and the plan

🔗

The company osteomyelitis keeps

ComorbidityHow it changes the diseaseHow it changes the management
Diabetes mellitusNeuropathy hides the ulcer; hyperglycaemia cripples neutrophil chemotaxis and oxidative burst; microvascular disease impairs delivery. Infections are more often polymicrobial, more often afebrile, and progress with fewer warning signs.Tight-ish glycaemic control; off-loading is non-negotiable; probe-to-bone at every visit; early surgical and vascular consultation; annual comprehensive foot exam for life. Expect a normal WBC and no fever — do not be reassured by them.
Peripheral arterial disease / critical limb ischaemiaThe rate-limiting step for healing and for antibiotic delivery. Converts a treatable infection into a limb-threatening one.Assess perfusion in every foot — and remember the ABI is falsely normal in diabetes/CKD (medial calcification); use toe pressures or TcPO₂. Urgent joint vascular + surgical consultation (IWGDF/IDSA 2023). Revascularisation may do more than any antibiotic.
CKD / ESRD on haemodialysisRecurrent S. aureus bacteraemia from vascular access → a leading cause of vertebral osteomyelitis. Uraemia blunts immunity.Renal dosing of nearly everything (vancomycin, cefepime, levofloxacin, TMP-SMX). Cefepime accumulates and causes non-convulsive status epilepticus if not dose-reduced. Linezolid and doxycycline need no renal adjustment — often the pragmatic choice. Coordinate dosing with dialysis sessions.
Injection drug useUnusual axial sites (sternoclavicular, sacroiliac, pubic symphysis); MRSA and Pseudomonas; frequent concurrent endocarditis; high risk of relapse from ongoing use.Get an echocardiogram. OPAT with a central line is a genuine risk (line misuse) — this is exactly the patient in whom the OVIVA oral strategy is most valuable. Engage addiction medicine; start MOUD (buprenorphine/methadone) during the admission. Note rifampin dramatically lowers methadone levels and can precipitate withdrawal.
Immunosuppression / transplant / chronic steroidsBlunts fever and leukocytosis; broadens the organism list to fungi, NTM, Nocardia. Impairs healing.Lower threshold to biopsy and to request AFB/fungal cultures. Steroids also mask the CRP response. Watch drug–drug interactions: rifampin will collapse tacrolimus, ciclosporin and sirolimus levels — a transplant patient on rifampin needs level monitoring and dose escalation.
Sickle cell diseaseSalmonella (and S. aureus). Bone infarction provides the nidus, and vaso-occlusive crisis is clinically indistinguishable from acute osteomyelitis.Do not assume crisis. MRI and cultures separate them. Cover both Salmonella (ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone) and S. aureus empirically until cultures return.
Orthopaedic hardware / prosthetic jointBiofilm on an abiotic surface. Low-virulence organisms (coagulase-negative staph, Cutibacterium) become true pathogens. Cure without removing the hardware is difficult.Add rifampin once staph is confirmed and bacteraemia has cleared. Decide explicitly with orthopaedics: retain (DAIR) vs one-stage vs two-stage exchange vs suppression. Hold cultures 10–14 days for Cutibacterium.
Malnutrition / hypoalbuminaemiaWound healing and immune function are anabolic — without substrate, neither happens. Predicts surgical failure.Dietitian referral; protein and calorie supplementation; correct vitamin C, zinc and vitamin D deficiency. This is cheap and routinely forgotten.
Tobacco useVasoconstriction plus impaired osteoblast function and fracture/wound healing. A major driver of debridement failure and non-union.Cessation is a genuine therapeutic intervention here, not a box-tick. USPSTF Grade A: offer behavioural intervention plus FDA-approved pharmacotherapy.
Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathyThe great mimic. Produces a red, hot, swollen foot with marrow oedema on MRI and bone destruction on plain film — with no infection at all.The distinction that saves limbs. Charcot is typically midfoot, without an ulcer or portal of entry; osteomyelitis is typically under an ulcer at a pressure point. When MRI can't settle it, use labelled-WBC scintigraphy with marrow subtraction — leukocytes accumulate in infection but not in Charcot marrow expansion. Do not amputate a Charcot foot for an infection it doesn't have.
Drugs to avoid or use with real caution in osteomyelitis
  • Rifampin as monotherapy — never. Resistance emerges within days. It is an add-on only, after bacteraemia has cleared, and always with a companion drug. It is also a potent CYP450 inducer: it will render warfarin, DOACs, oral contraceptives, statins, tacrolimus/ciclosporin, HIV protease inhibitors and methadone ineffective or sub-therapeutic.
  • Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam together — this combination carries a well-described increase in acute kidney injury above either agent alone. If you need broad gram-negative cover alongside vancomycin, consider cefepime or a carbapenem instead, and monitor creatinine closely.
  • Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant — it does not work for pneumonia. Fine for bone and bloodstream; useless in the lung. Monitor CK weekly, and stop it if myopathy develops (especially alongside a statin).
  • Linezolid — myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia, anaemia) rises with duration beyond ~2 weeks, so check a CBC weekly. It is a weak MAO inhibitor: risk of serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/SNRIs/tramadol/triptans. Peripheral and optic neuropathy occur with prolonged use.
  • Fluoroquinolones — tendinopathy and tendon rupture (worse with steroids and in the elderly), aortic aneurysm/dissection, QT prolongation, CNS effects, dysglycaemia, and C. difficile. They remain indispensable in bone infection because of their bioavailability, but the risk conversation is real. Absorption is destroyed by calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc, antacids and sucralfate — separate doses by at least 2 hours or the drug simply will not be absorbed.
  • Aminoglycosides — poor bone penetration, nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Not a sensible backbone for a 6-week bone course.
  • Antibiotics for a clinically uninfected ulcer — IWGDF/IDSA 2023 recommends against this. It does not prevent infection, does not speed healing, and does select resistance.
  • Cefepime in unadjusted renal failure — accumulates and causes neurotoxicity, including non-convulsive status epilepticus. Check the eGFR before you write the dose.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B recommendations relevant to this population

Osteomyelitis itself has no screening test. But the population that gets it — people with diabetes, vascular disease, tobacco use and injection drug use — is dense with Grade A and B preventive care, and clinic is where that happens.

GradeRecommendationPopulation & relevance here
ATobacco smoking cessation — ask all adults about tobacco use, advise quitting, and provide both behavioural intervention and FDA-approved pharmacotherapyAll adults. Smoking causes vasoconstriction and impairs osteoblast function and wound healing — it is a direct driver of debridement failure and non-union.
BScreening for prediabetes and type 2 diabetesAdults aged 35–70 years with overweight or obesity. Diabetes is the dominant risk factor for the osteomyelitis you will actually see. Offer/refer those with prediabetes to preventive interventions.
AScreening for hypertensionAdults ≥18. Drives the same vascular disease that dooms the diabetic foot.
BStatin for primary prevention of CVDAdults 40–75 with ≥1 CVD risk factor and an estimated 10-year risk ≥10%. Most diabetic-foot patients qualify.
BBehavioural counselling — healthy diet & physical activityAdults with CVD risk factors, including diabetes and dyslipidaemia.
BIntensive behavioural interventions for obesityAdults with BMI ≥30.
AHIV screeningAdolescents and adults 15–65 (and all pregnant persons). Relevant in injection drug use, and immunosuppression broadens the organism list.
BHepatitis C screeningAdults 18–79. High yield in people who inject drugs — the same population presenting with vertebral and sternoclavicular osteomyelitis.
IScreening for PAD with the ABI in asymptomatic adults — INSUFFICIENT evidenceNote carefully: this "I" statement applies to asymptomatic screening. It does not apply to your patient with a diabetic foot ulcer — in that patient, assessing perfusion is a diagnostic necessity, and IWGDF/IDSA 2023 requires it.
Not USPSTF, but arguably the highest-yield prevention in this diseaseThe annual comprehensive diabetic foot examination — inspection, monofilament and vibration testing for neuropathy, pedal pulses and perfusion assessment, footwear review, and patient education on daily self-inspection — is an ADA Standards of Care recommendation rather than a USPSTF one, but it is the intervention that actually prevents the ulcer that becomes the osteomyelitis. Perform it, document it, and escalate the frequency (every 3–6 months) in anyone with neuropathy, deformity, PAD, or a previous ulcer or amputation.
Every patient who has had a diabetic foot osteomyelitis is permanently high-risk for another. Off-loading footwear, podiatry, and structured surveillance after the infection resolves are not optional aftercare — they are the treatment for the next episode.
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags — "don't manage this in clinic"

Send to the ED now — these cannot wait for a clinic slot:
  • Any new neurological deficit with back pain — weakness, sensory level, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence. This is a spinal epidural abscess with cord compression until an MRI says otherwise. Emergent whole-spine MRI + neurosurgery, the same hour. Neurological recovery is a function of how fast the cord is decompressed; a deficit that has been present for hours may recover, one present for days often will not.
  • Sepsis — fever with hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnoea, confusion, or a raised lactate. Grade 4 (severe) diabetic foot infection by IWGDF/IDSA criteria.
  • Crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis, pain out of proportion, rapid spread — necrotising soft-tissue infection. This is a surgical emergency; the operating theatre is the diagnostic test, not the MRI.
  • Extensive gangrene, deep (below-fascia) abscess, or compartment syndrome — IWGDF/IDSA 2023 mandates urgent surgical consultation.
  • Critical limb ischaemia — a cold, pulseless, dusky foot with rest pain. Urgent vascular consultation; the limb is on a clock.
Admit (but not emergently):
  • Severe (grade 4) diabetic foot infection, or moderate (grade 3) with relevant morbidities — IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Recommendation 2.
  • Need for urgent surgical debridement or revascularisation.
  • Need for IV antibiotics that cannot be delivered as OPAT.
  • Failure of appropriately-dosed outpatient therapy — worsening wound, rising CRP, spreading erythema.
  • Inability to manage at home: no off-loading possible, cannot access dressings, poor adherence, unsafe home, no support.
  • Metabolic decompensation — DKA, hyperosmolar state, AKI.
  • Suspected vertebral osteomyelitis needing an image-guided biopsy that cannot be arranged promptly as an outpatient.
The one you cannot afford to miss: a patient with back pain, fever, and a raised CRP who is sent home with analgesia. The classic triad of back pain + fever + neurological deficit is present in only a minority of spinal epidural abscess cases — waiting for all three is how the diagnosis is missed. If a patient has new, severe, unrelenting back pain plus any reason to be bacteraemic (IVDU, dialysis, recent staph bacteraemia, indwelling line, recent spinal procedure), get the ESR/CRP and get the MRI.
🛏️ Wards — inpatient diagnosis, source control & the antibiotic course
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria

Admit if…Threshold / detail
Severe (grade 4) diabetic foot infectionAny foot infection plus ≥2 SIRS criteria (T >38 or <36 °C; HR >90; RR >20 or PaCO₂ <32 mmHg; WBC >12,000 or <4,000/mm³ or >10% bands). IWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 2.
Moderate (grade 3) infection with relevant morbidityDeep infection or erythema ≥2 cm, plus severe PAD, poor glycaemic control, inability to self-care, or failure of outpatient therapy. IWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 2.
Needs urgent surgical source controlDeep abscess, necrotising infection, extensive gangrene, compartment syndrome, septic arthritis. Early surgery within 24–48 h is recommended for moderate/severe DFI (IWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 20).
Needs revascularisationInfected foot + PAD → urgent joint vascular and surgical consultation (IWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 21).
Suspected native vertebral osteomyelitisFor urgent MRI, blood cultures, and an image-guided bone biopsy — most of which cannot be assembled quickly as an outpatient.
S. aureus bacteraemiaAlways an inpatient problem: needs source hunting, an echocardiogram, repeat blood cultures documenting clearance, and ID consultation.
IV therapy that cannot be given as OPATNo line access, no home infusion service, unsafe housing, active injection drug use with line-misuse risk, or cognitive impairment.
Failed appropriate outpatient therapyWorsening wound, spreading erythema, rising CRP, or no improvement after ~4 weeks of apparently adequate treatment (IWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 12d → re-evaluate).
Metabolic decompensationDKA, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, AKI, severe hyperglycaemia that cannot be controlled at home.
Admission is not the same as "start antibiotics immediately." Admit the well patient with suspected osteomyelitis so that you can get the biopsy properly — then hold antibiotics until the sample is in the pot (IDSA 2015). The patient is in a hospital bed being observed; a 24–72 hour wait for a culture-directed regimen is safe and it will change the next six weeks of their life.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

Labs, imaging, cultures, consults

Blood cultures ×2BEFORE the first antibiotic dose, from two separate sites. The highest-yield order on this list — a positive S. aureus/S. lugdunensis/Brucella culture with a concordant MRI can spare the patient a biopsy entirely (IDSA 2015 Rec 15).STAT
CBC, CRP, ESRBaseline for the trend you will follow for the next six weeks. Expect the ESR/CRP to be up and the WBC to be normal.Admit
BMP / creatinine + eGFR, LFTs, albuminYou cannot dose vancomycin, cefepime or levofloxacin without the renal function. Albumin predicts healing.Admit
HbA1c, glucose, ± ketones/VBGEvery diabetic-foot patient. Rule out DKA/HHS in the unwell.Admit
LactateIf any SIRS criteria or suspicion of sepsis. Drives the sepsis bundle and the ICU conversation.If SIRS
Plain radiograph of the siteEveryone. Baseline; detects gas, foreign body, fracture, Charcot, and established sequestrum/involucrum.Admit
MRI with contrastThe test of choice. Order it emergently (whole spine) if there is any neurological deficit. In vertebral osteomyelitis, image the whole spine — skip lesions at non-contiguous levels are well described and will change the operation.Urgent
BONE biopsy + culture + histopathologyImage-guided or intra-operative. Send both micro and histology. Specify AFB and fungal cultures if the course is indolent; ask the lab to hold cultures 10–14 days if Cutibacterium is possible (shoulder hardware).Definitive
Echocardiogram (TTE → TOE)If S. aureus, streptococcal or enterococcal bacteraemia, injection drug use, or haematogenous disease with no obvious source. Vertebral osteomyelitis and endocarditis coexist far more often than people expect.If bacteraemic
Vascular studies — ABI, toe pressures, TcPO₂Every diabetic/PAD foot. Remember ABI is falsely normal in medial calcification — use toe pressures.DFO
Consults: Orthopaedics / Surgery, Infectious Diseases, Vascular, Podiatry, EndocrineOsteomyelitis is a team disease. Urgent surgical consult for severe infection or moderate infection with gangrene, necrotising infection, deep abscess, compartment syndrome or severe ischaemia (IWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 19).Day 1
Off-loading order + wound careWritten explicitly: strict non-weight-bearing / total-contact cast / heel protectors. It will not happen unless you order it. Air-mattress and turning schedule for pressure ulcers.Day 1
VTE prophylaxis, glycaemic protocol, nutrition, analgesiaThe bread and butter. Bone pain is severe — treat it properly. Dietitian referral if albumin is low.Admit
Do not send a superficial wound or sinus-tract swab and treat the result. It grows colonising flora that correlates poorly with the true bone pathogen. IWGDF/IDSA 2023 explicitly recommends obtaining bone — not soft tissue — for culture. If you must culture soft tissue, take a deep tissue specimen by curettage or biopsy after debridement, aseptically — not a cotton swab across the surface.
Treat

Acute inpatient management

💊

The four-step inpatient ladder

1
Cultures first — then decide whether to hold antibiotics
The decision that shapes the whole admission
▾
Stable — normal, stable neuro exam and stable haemodynamics? → Draw blood cultures, arrange the biopsy, and HOLD antibiotics until a microbiological diagnosis is established (IDSA 2015 Rec 24; holding for 1–2 weeks where feasible is reasonable). A culture-directed regimen is worth vastly more than a 48-hour head start on a disease you are going to treat for six weeks.

Septic, or any neurological deficit? → Do not wait. Blood cultures, then empiric antibiotics immediately, then biopsy/surgery as soon as feasible. In sepsis, every hour of delay costs mortality.
2
Empiric antibiotics — when you cannot wait
Let the clinical scenario pick the organism
▾
Empiric cover follows the clinical scenario, because the scenario predicts the organism. Everything funnels to the same endpoint: narrow on culture.
ScenarioEmpiric regimenRationale
Vertebral osteomyelitis, septic or with a neuro deficitVancomycin (15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h, AUC-guided) + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h (or cefepime 2 g IV q8–12h if Pseudomonas risk)Covers MRSA plus streptococci and Enterobacterales — the realistic organism set for haematogenous spinal disease. Narrow the moment cultures return.
Severe (grade 4) diabetic foot infectionVancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g IV q6h) or vancomycin + a carbapenem (meropenem 1 g IV q8h / ertapenem 1 g IV q24h)Broad gram-positive + gram-negative + anaerobic cover for a limb- and life-threatening polymicrobial infection. Note the vancomycin + pip-tazo AKI signal — if renal function is fragile, prefer cefepime or a carbapenem for the gram-negative half.
Moderate (grade 3) diabetic foot infectionAmpicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV q6h, or amoxicillin-clavulanate PO; add MRSA cover only if there are risk factorsCovers streptococci, MSSA, Enterobacterales and anaerobes. IWGDF/IDSA 2023 advises against empiric anti-pseudomonal cover in temperate climates unless Pseudomonas was recently isolated or the setting is tropical/subtropical.
Mild (grade 2) diabetic foot infection, no recent antibiotics, temperate climateTarget aerobic gram-positives only — cephalexin, flucloxacillin, or amoxicillin-clavulanate POIWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 14: β-haemolytic streptococci and S. aureus (including MRSA if indicated) are the pathogens that matter here. Do not reach for a carbapenem.
Post-operative / hardware-associatedVancomycin + an anti-pseudomonal β-lactam (cefepime or pip-tazo). Add rifampin only after staph is confirmed and bacteraemia has cleared.Covers MRSA, coagulase-negative staph and gram-negatives. Rifampin is the biofilm agent — but adding it too early (during bacteraemia, or before you know the bug) risks selecting rifampin resistance for no benefit.
Injection drug useVancomycin + an anti-pseudomonal β-lactam (cefepime 2 g IV q8h)MRSA and Pseudomonas are both realistic. Get the echocardiogram.
Sickle cell diseaseCeftriaxone 2 g IV q24h (± vancomycin)Covers Salmonella — and add staph cover, because S. aureus is still common. Distinguishing this from vaso-occlusive crisis is the real work.
Empiric therapy is a bridge, not a destination. Write the de-escalation plan in the same note in which you write the empiric regimen: "Vanc + cefepime pending bone culture — narrow at 48–72 h." Otherwise the patient will still be on both drugs at discharge because nobody felt authorised to stop them.
3
Source control — the step that actually cures
Antibiotics do not dissolve dead bone
▾

Return to the pathophysiology: the sequestrum has no blood supply, and the biofilm on it is metabolically dormant. No dose, no duration, and no route of any antibiotic will sterilise it. Debridement is the therapy; the antibiotic protects the debrided bed.

IndicationUrgencySource
Necrotising soft-tissue infection, gas, compartment syndrome, extensive gangrene, deep (below-fascia) abscessImmediate — theatre nowIWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 19: urgent surgical consultation. Do not delay for imaging.
Spinal epidural abscess with a neurological deficitEmergent — same hourIDSA 2015 Rec 28: surgical intervention for progressive neurological deficits, progressive deformity, or spinal instability. Recovery is time-dependent.
Moderate/severe diabetic foot infection needing debridementEarly — within 24–48 hIWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 20.
Infected foot ulcer/gangrene + PADUrgent joint vascular + surgical consultIWGDF/IDSA 2023 Rec 21 — to decide the timing of drainage and revascularisation.
Persistent or recurrent bacteraemia (no other source), or worsening pain despite appropriate therapyConsider debridement ± stabilisationIDSA 2015 Rec 29.
Sequestrum, sinus tract, or chronic osteomyelitisElective but essentialChronic osteomyelitis without debridement relapses. Plan the operation; don't just extend the antibiotics.
Worsening bony imaging at 4–6 weeks but the patient is clinically improving with falling markersDo NOT operateIDSA 2015 Rec 30 explicitly advises against surgery in this situation. Bone imaging lags clinical healing. Treat the patient, not the picture.

Beyond debridement, the surgeon is also solving dead space and coverage: antibiotic-loaded cement beads or spacers, local antibiotic carriers, muscle or free flaps to bring vascularised tissue into the defect, external fixation and bone transport for Cierny–Mader IV disease, and — when appropriate — amputation.

4
Narrow, set the duration, and plan the exit
Restart the clock at the last debridement
▾

Once the culture is back: narrow the regimen, count the duration from the last debridement (see the timeline in the Clinic panel), and decide the route. Thanks to OVIVA (NEJM 2019), the route can very often be oral — and an early oral switch means no line, no line infection, and often a discharge several weeks earlier.

Can this patient switch to oral? All four must be true:
  1. Source control achieved — the dead bone and pus are out, or there was none.
  2. Clinically improving — afebrile, pain settling, CRP falling, bacteraemia cleared (documented negative blood cultures if it was ever positive).
  3. A susceptible organism with a highly bioavailable oral option — fluoroquinolone, linezolid, TMP-SMX, doxycycline, clindamycin, or a high-dose oral β-lactam.
  4. A reliable patient who will absorb and take it — no vomiting, no malabsorption, no interacting binder (calcium/iron/antacids kill quinolone absorption), and adherent.
If all four hold, switch. If not, arrange OPAT.

IDSA 2015 unless noted
Dose at the top of the rangeIWGDF/IDSA 2023 explicitly advises administering antibiotics for bone infection at their upper recommended dosage range, because penetration from blood into bone is the rate-limiting step. This is not the place to be conservative with dosing — it is the place to be conservative with spectrum.

MSSA — methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (the commonest result you will get)
