Three de-escalations worth writing on your list every morning: (1) MSSA on vancomycin → switch to cefazolin or nafcillin, always; vancomycin is inferior for MSSA. (2) Broad empiric cover with a culture back for 48 h → narrow. (3) An IV line still in place in a patient meeting all four oral-switch criteria → take it out; every line-day is a line-infection risk.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend every day

TrendCadenceWhat "good" looks like — and what should worry you
Pain & functionDailyShould steadily improve. Escalating pain despite appropriate therapy is a surgical question, not an analgesic one — IDSA 2015 lists worsening pain as an indication to consider debridement.
Neurological exam (if vertebral)Every shiftPower, sensation, reflexes, perineal sensation, bladder function. Any new deficit → emergent MRI + neurosurgery. This is the single most important repeated examination on the ward.
Wound / ulcerDailySize, depth, exudate, surrounding erythema, granulation. Photograph it. Spreading erythema or new necrosis means the source is not controlled.
CRPEvery 2–3 days, then weeklyShould be falling. A flat or rising CRP after the first few days should make you ask: undrained pus? wrong bug? wrong drug? resistant organism?
Temperature, HR, BP, lactatePer obs; lactate if unwellPersistent fever >72 h on appropriate antibiotics = undrained collection until proven otherwise. Get the imaging.
Repeat blood culturesIf S. aureus bacteraemia — every 48–72 h until negativeDocumented clearance is mandatory. Persistent bacteraemia after 72 h of appropriate therapy = a deep, undrained source (endocarditis, epidural abscess, septic thrombophlebitis, retained hardware). And you cannot start rifampin until the blood is sterile.
Creatinine / eGFR≥2×/week on vancomycin; more if unstableVancomycin AKI, especially with pip-tazo. Re-dose everything renally-cleared when the eGFR moves.
Vancomycin levels / AUCPer pharmacy protocolTarget AUC₂₄/MIC 400–600. Under-dosing fails; over-dosing (AUC >600) causes nephrotoxicity.
CKWeekly on daptomycinStop for myopathy or CK >~5× ULN.
CBCWeekly on linezolid, nafcillin or prolonged β-lactamLinezolid thrombocytopenia/anaemia; β-lactam neutropenia.
LFTsEvery 2 weeks on rifampinRifampin hepatotoxicity.
GlucosePer protocolHyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function — control it as part of the infection treatment, not as a side quest.
Off-loading adherenceDaily, with your own eyesWritten orders are not the same as an off-loaded foot. Look. Every step on that ulcer undoes the debridement.
Not getting better? Work through this list before you widen the antibiotics: (1) Undrained pus or retained dead bone — by far the most common answer; re-image and call the surgeon. (2) The wrong organism — you are treating a swab, or you missed TB/fungus/Brucella/Cutibacterium. (3) The drug isn't getting there — under-dosed, poor bone penetration, oral drug not absorbed (a quinolone taken with calcium is a placebo), or an ischaemic limb with no delivery at all. (4) Retained hardware with biofilm and no rifampin. (5) It isn't infection — Charcot, gout, fracture, tumour. Broadening the antibiotic fixes none of these five.
Tool

Renal dosing helper

🧮

Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance → antibiotic dose adjustment

Nearly every antibiotic in this guide is renally cleared, and getting the dose wrong is one of the more common real harms in a six-week course. Cockcroft–Gault is the formula most antibiotic dosing tables were built on.

Age (years)

Weight (kg)

Serum creatinine (mg/dL)

Sex

—
Enter age, weight, creatinine and sex.
CrCl = [(140 − age) × weight(kg)] ÷ (72 × SCr), × 0.85 if female. Cockcroft DW, Gault MH. Nephron 1976. Uses actual body weight — in significant obesity, many pharmacies use adjusted body weight; check your local protocol. This estimates clearance only; it does not replace pharmacy-led AUC-guided vancomycin dosing.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Numeric escalation triggers

Call the ICU — floor → unit:
  • Hypotension requiring a vasopressor — MAP <65 mmHg after ≥30 mL/kg crystalloid. This is septic shock by Sepsis-3 definition when accompanied by lactate >2 mmol/L.
  • Lactate >4 mmol/L, or a lactate that is rising despite resuscitation.
  • qSOFA ≥2 (RR ≥22, altered mentation, SBP ≤100) — see the ICU panel calculator. Not a diagnostic test, but a strong prompt to escalate care.
  • Respiratory failure — RR >30, SpO₂ <92% on ≥6 L, rising FiO₂ requirement, or any need for NIV/intubation.
  • New or progressive neurological deficit from spinal epidural abscess — cord compression is a neurosurgical emergency, and these patients often need ICU-level monitoring peri-operatively.
  • Necrotising soft-tissue infection — going to theatre for extensive debridement, or already there.
  • Acute kidney injury needing renal replacement, or rapidly rising creatinine with oliguria.
  • Persistent S. aureus bacteraemia >72 h with haemodynamic instability — implies an undrained focus and impending decompensation.
  • DKA or hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state requiring an insulin infusion, in a hospital where that requires ICU/step-down.
Cord compression is measured in hours. A patient with vertebral osteomyelitis who develops new weakness, a sensory level, saddle anaesthesia or urinary retention needs an emergent MRI of the whole spine and a neurosurgical decision the same hour. Do not book it for the morning list. Functional recovery correlates directly with how long the cord has been compressed, and a deficit that has been present for days frequently does not recover at all.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness, OPAT, and where they go

Discharge readiness — all of these:

  • Source control achieved. Debridement done; no undrained collection on the most recent imaging. If dead bone was left behind deliberately, that decision is documented and the duration reflects it.
  • Haemodynamically stable and afebrile ≥24–48 h.
  • Bacteraemia cleared — documented negative blood cultures if they were ever positive.
  • CRP falling and pain improving.
  • The complete antibiotic plan is written down: the drug, the dose, the route, the stop date (counted from the last debridement), the monitoring bloods and their frequency, and who is chasing them.
  • The route is deliverable — either the patient meets all four oral-switch criteria, or OPAT is fully arranged (line in, nursing organised, bloods booked, ID follow-up in the diary).
  • Off-loading and wound care are in place, with the equipment physically in the patient's possession.
  • Follow-up booked: ID/OPAT clinic, surgery, podiatry, vascular, diabetes.
OPAT vs oral — the OVIVA questionBefore you commit a patient to six weeks with a PICC line, ask honestly whether they meet the four oral-switch criteria. OVIVA showed oral is non-inferior — and a line avoided is a line infection, a DVT, a readmission and a district-nurse visit avoided. Reserve OPAT for patients who genuinely have no bioavailable oral option (e.g. a resistant gram-negative with no oral agent) or who cannot absorb/adhere. In a person who injects drugs, an indwelling central line carries real risk of misuse — this is precisely the patient in whom the oral strategy is most valuable.

Home

Independent, stable, reliable. On oral antibiotics with a written stop date. Can off-load and manage the dressing. Bloods and clinic follow-up booked.

Home + OPAT / home health

Needs IV therapy but is otherwise well. Line in, home infusion arranged, district nursing for dressings, weekly bloods (CBC, CRP, creatinine, ± CK/LFTs) with a named clinician reviewing them, and ID follow-up.

SNF / skilled nursing

Needs 24-hour skilled nursing for IV antibiotics, complex wound care or non-weight-bearing that they cannot maintain at home. Fewer than ~3 h of therapy per day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-amputation or post-spinal-surgery with a neurological deficit, who can tolerate ≥3 h of therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines and has clear rehab potential (prosthetic training, gait re-education).

LTAC

Prolonged, complex care — multiple planned debridements, ventilator weaning after ICU, or extensive wound management expected to exceed ~25 days.

Palliative / hospice

Cierny–Mader class C: curative treatment would be worse than the disease. Chronic suppressive antibiotics or comfort-focused care. A legitimate, guideline-recognised plan — not a failure.
The most common discharge failure in osteomyelitis is not a wrong drug — it is a missing stop date and an unowned blood test. Write the stop date in the discharge summary, in the OPAT referral, and in the patient's own copy. Name the clinician responsible for the weekly bloods. Otherwise you will meet this patient again in six weeks, still on linezolid, now pancytopenic.
🫀 ICU — sepsis from a bone source, cord compression & emergency source control
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

Why osteomyelitis lands in the unit

Osteomyelitis itself is an indolent disease — it does not usually put people in an ICU bed. When it does, it is almost always one of four things, and each has a different clock:

ReasonThe problemThe clock
1. Septic shock from the bone/soft-tissue sourceUsually a severe (grade 4) diabetic foot infection, an undrained abscess, or ongoing S. aureus bacteraemia ± endocarditis. Vasoplegia, lactataemia, organ dysfunction.Hours. Sepsis bundle + source control. Antibiotics do not fix undrained pus.
2. Spinal epidural abscess with cord compressionPus in the epidural space compressing the cord, or septic thrombophlebitis infarcting it. Presents as weakness, sensory level, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention.Hours — and recovery is time-dependent. Emergent whole-spine MRI + neurosurgery now. Not the morning list.
3. Necrotising soft-tissue infectionOverlapping with severe diabetic foot infection. Crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis, pain out of proportion, rapid spread, systemic toxicity.Immediate theatre. The operating room is the diagnostic test — do not wait for an MRI to confirm what your hands already told you.
4. Post-operative critical careAfter a big debridement, spinal decompression/instrumentation, or a major amputation — for haemodynamic and neurological monitoring, transfusion and analgesia.Planned. Expect blood loss and pain.

qSOFA — quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment

A three-item bedside screen (Sepsis-3, JAMA 2016). It is not a diagnostic test for sepsis and it is not sensitive enough to rule sepsis out — but a qSOFA ≥2 in a patient with suspected infection identifies someone at markedly higher risk of a poor outcome and should prompt escalation, a lactate, and a hard look at whether they belong on the floor.

0
qSOFA points (0–3)
Tick any criteria that are present.
Singer M, et al. The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). JAMA. 2016;315(8):801–810. Septic shock = sepsis + vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation. For the full SOFA score, use MDCalc — it is a continuous multi-organ score and is not reproduced here.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

WhatWhenTarget / why
Arterial lineAny patient on a vasopressorBeat-to-beat MAP and easy repeated gases/lactates. Non-invasive cuffs are unreliable in vasoplegia.
Central venous accessFor vasopressors, and for the long antibiotic courseNorepinephrine can be run peripherally for a short period through a good proximal line while central access is obtained — but do not let that become the plan.
MAPContinuous≥65 mmHg — the Surviving Sepsis default. Individualise upward in chronic hypertension or in cord compression, where spinal cord perfusion pressure matters and many neurosurgeons will ask for a higher MAP target post-decompression.
LactateOn arrival, then q2–4h until clearingGuide resuscitation to lactate clearance. A rising lactate on adequate pressors means an undrained source, not more fluid.
Urine outputHourly>0.5 mL/kg/h. Falling output is both a perfusion signal and an antibiotic-dosing problem.
Repeat blood culturesq48h until negative if S. aureus bacteraemiaPersistent bacteraemia beyond 72 h of appropriate therapy means an undrained focus — epidural abscess, endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, retained hardware, a metastatic collection. Go and find it.
Neurological examHourly if there is any cord/cauda concernPower, sensory level, perineal sensation, anal tone, bladder. A new deficit is an emergency, at any hour. Document it so a change is detectable.
Creatinine, CK, CBC, LFTs, vancomycin AUCDaily in the unitEvery antibiotic here has an organ toxicity, and the ICU patient's clearance changes daily. Re-dose to today's renal function, not admission's.
Glucoseq1–2h on an insulin infusionHyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function; hypoglycaemia kills. Follow the unit protocol.
EchocardiogramTTE, then TOE if negative and suspicion persistsS. aureus bacteraemia with a bone focus should always prompt a search for endocarditis — it changes duration, may need surgery, and predicts relapse.
Support

Pressors & inotropes

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

Septic shock from a bone or foot source is distributive shock: pathogen-associated molecular patterns drive iNOS, nitric oxide floods the vasculature, vascular smooth muscle loses tone, and systemic vascular resistance collapses. The cardiac output is typically high. So the therapeutic problem is vasoplegia, and the drug you want is a vasoconstrictor — not an inotrope.

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHaemodynamic effectWhen to pick it
Norepinephrine
FIRST-LINE		α₁ ≫ β₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min (titrate to MAP; higher doses used in refractory shock)↑↑ SVR, modest ↑ contractility, minimal chronotropyThe first-line vasopressor in septic shock (Surviving Sepsis). It fixes the exact lesion — lost vascular tone — with less tachyarrhythmia than dopamine or epinephrine.
Vasopressin
SECOND		V₁ receptors on vascular smooth muscle — a completely non-adrenergic pathwayFixed 0.03 units/min (not titrated)↑ SVR; no direct inotropy or chronotropyAdd to norepinephrine to raise the MAP and spare catecholamine dose. Works when adrenergic receptors are downregulated by acidosis and prolonged catecholamine exposure — a different lever on the same problem. Relative vasopressin deficiency is well described in septic shock.
Epinephrine
THIRD		α₁ + β₁ + β₂0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑ SVR, ↑↑ contractility, ↑↑ heart rateAdd when the MAP is still inadequate on norepinephrine + vasopressin, or when there is coexisting myocardial dysfunction (septic cardiomyopathy). Expect tachyarrhythmia and a rise in lactate from β₂-driven glycolysis — that lactate is metabolic, not necessarily worsening hypoperfusion. Don't chase it.
Dobutamine
INOTROPE — only if pump failure		β₁ ≫ β₂2.5–20 mcg/kg/min↑↑ contractility, ↑ CO, ↓ SVR (β₂ vasodilation)Only for septic cardiomyopathy — persistent hypoperfusion with a documented low cardiac output despite adequate MAP and volume. It will drop the blood pressure in a vasoplegic patient — always run it alongside a vasopressor.
PhenylephrinePure α₁0.5–6 mcg/kg/min↑ SVR, reflex bradycardia, may ↓ CONiche. Useful when tachyarrhythmia makes norepinephrine untenable. Not a first-line agent in sepsis.
Hydrocortisone
ADJUNCT		Restores vascular responsiveness to catecholamines (upregulates adrenergic receptors); anti-inflammatory200 mg/day IV — as 50 mg q6h or a continuous infusionFaster shock reversal; hastens vasopressor weaningConsider in septic shock with an ongoing vasopressor requirement despite adequate fluid and pressors. Speeds shock reversal; the mortality signal is less certain.
Match the drug to the lesion. In distributive shock the pipes are too wide, so you need an α₁ agonist to narrow them — norepinephrine. Vasopressin attacks the same problem through a different receptor, which is why it works when the adrenergic system is exhausted. An inotrope (dobutamine) is the right answer only when the pump is genuinely failing — and giving it to a vasoplegic patient will make the blood pressure worse, because β₂ stimulation vasodilates further.
No vasopressor will fix undrained pus. If you find yourself escalating to a third pressor in a patient with a severe foot infection or a spinal collection, the problem is almost certainly that source control has not happened. The most important drug in septic shock from osteomyelitis is a surgeon.
Airway

Respiratory support

🌬️

When they need the ventilator, and how to set it

Osteomyelitis is not a lung disease — respiratory failure here is always secondary. Know which of the four causes you are dealing with, because the fix differs:

  • Sepsis-induced ARDS — the commonest. Diffuse inflammatory lung injury from a distant infective source. Treat with lung-protective ventilation and by controlling the source.
  • Septic pulmonary emboli — from right-sided endocarditis or septic thrombophlebitis (e.g. a Lemierre-type picture, or an infected line). Look for peripheral nodules with cavitation on CT.
  • High cervical cord compression — a lesion at or above C3–C5 knocks out the phrenic nerves and the diaphragm. This is a neurological emergency presenting as respiratory failure; watch the vital capacity, not just the saturation.
  • Peri-operative — post-debridement, post-spinal instrumentation, prolonged prone positioning.
NIV or intubate? NIV has a limited role here. It may buy time in a cooperative patient with cardiogenic or hypercapnic overlay — but it is not appropriate in the patient with a depressed conscious level, shock, a full stomach heading to theatre, or an ascending cord lesion. Intubate for a falling GCS, refractory hypoxaemia, exhaustion, haemodynamic collapse, or a high cord lesion with a falling vital capacity. Beware: induction agents cause profound hypotension in vasoplegic patients — have the pressor running before you push the drug.

In ARDS from a septic bone source, the ventilator is supportive, not curative. The intervention that changes the trajectory is source control. If the oxygenation is deteriorating and the surgeon has not yet been to theatre, you are optimising the wrong variable.
Rescue

Emergency source control & rescue therapies

⚙️

The three that cannot wait until morning

1 — Spinal epidural abscess with cord compression.
  • Recognise: back pain + fever + a new neurological deficit. Only a minority have the full triad — waiting for all three is how this is missed.
  • Image: emergent MRI of the whole spine with contrast — skip lesions at non-contiguous levels are well described and will change the operation.
  • Act: neurosurgery now. Surgical decompression is indicated for progressive neurological deficit, progressive deformity, or spinal instability (IDSA 2015, Rec 28). Give antibiotics immediately after blood cultures — do not hold them for a biopsy in a patient with a deficit.
  • Understand the clock: neurological recovery is a direct function of how long the cord has been compressed and how complete the deficit is at the time of decompression. A deficit of hours may recover fully; one of days often will not. This is why "we'll do it on the morning list" is the wrong answer.
2 — Necrotising soft-tissue infection.
  • Recognise: pain out of proportion to the exam, crepitus, bullae, dusky/necrotic skin, rapid spread over hours, systemic toxicity out of keeping with the visible wound.
  • Act: the operating theatre is the diagnostic test. Do not delay surgery to obtain an MRI. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (a carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin) plus clindamycin, which suppresses ribosomal toxin production in streptococci and staphylococci — an antitoxin effect, not just an antibacterial one.
  • Expect repeated debridements every 24–48 h until the tissue stops advancing.
3 — Septic shock with an undrained focus.
  • Sepsis bundle: cultures before antibiotics (but never delay antibiotics in shock), broad-spectrum antibiotics within the hour, ≥30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4, then vasopressors to MAP ≥65, and serial lactates.
  • And then find the pus. A patient who does not improve, whose lactate will not clear, or who needs escalating pressors has a source you have not controlled. Re-image. Call the surgeon again.

Adjuncts and special situations

TherapyRole in osteomyelitis
Local antibiotic delivery — antibiotic-loaded cement beads/spacers, calcium-sulfate carriersDelivers very high local concentrations into the dead space that systemic therapy cannot reach, while keeping systemic levels low. An adjunct to debridement, never a substitute for it.
Negative-pressure wound therapy (VAC)Manages exudate, promotes granulation and reduces dead space between debridements. Again — it does not replace excision of dead bone.
Muscle / free flap coverageBrings vascularised tissue into an avascular defect. This is how you convert bone that antibiotics cannot reach into bone that they can — it is mechanistically an antimicrobial intervention.
RevascularisationIn the ischaemic diabetic foot, restoring perfusion may be the single highest-yield "antimicrobial" you can prescribe. Urgent joint vascular + surgical consultation (IWGDF/IDSA 2023).
Hyperbaric oxygenSometimes used for refractory chronic osteomyelitis and problem diabetic-foot wounds. The evidence base is weak and inconsistent; it is never a substitute for debridement and appropriate antibiotics. Do not let it delay the operation.
AmputationThe definitive source control when the limb cannot be salvaged. In a septic patient with a dead foot, a timely amputation is a life-saving operation, not a defeat.
Goals-of-care conversationThe Cierny–Mader class C host in an ICU bed deserves an honest conversation about whether cure is achievable at all. Suppression and comfort are legitimate plans.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

ICU → floor

Ready for the floor when ALL of these hold:
  • Off all vasopressors for ≥6–12 h with a MAP ≥65 mmHg.
  • Lactate normalised (<2 mmol/L) and staying down.
  • Extubated and maintaining SpO₂ ≥92% on ≤4 L nasal cannula, with a stable respiratory rate.
  • Source control is definitively achieved — the abscess is drained, the dead bone is out, the cord is decompressed. This is the one people skip.
  • Blood cultures clearing — documented negatives if there was S. aureus bacteraemia.
  • Neurologically stable — no progression of any deficit over ≥24 h, and a documented, reproducible baseline exam the ward team can compare against.
  • Renal function stable, not requiring RRT, and antibiotic doses adjusted to the current clearance.
  • A definitive antibiotic plan exists — the organism, the drug, the route, and the stop date counted from the last debridement.
Not yet — hold them in the unit if: the surgeon is planning a further "look and debride" in the next 24–48 h; the blood cultures are still positive; there is any new or progressing neurological deficit; the vasopressor was stopped less than 6 hours ago; the lactate is still drifting up; or the source control was partial and everyone is quietly hoping the antibiotics will finish the job. That last one is the classic bounce-back — a patient downgraded with an undrained collection will be back within 48 hours, sicker.
Before you transfer, write the neurological baseline in plain language in the handover — "moves all four limbs against gravity, sensation intact to T10, no saddle anaesthesia, voiding spontaneously." The ward team's job for the next six weeks is to notice when that changes, and they can only do that if you told them what it was.
Pearls

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The fifteen things that actually change what you do

  1. Dead bone does not take antibiotics. The sequestrum is avascular — no dose, duration or route reaches it. Chronic osteomyelitis is a surgical disease with an antibiotic adjunct. If you find yourself on week eight of antibiotics with no surgical plan, you have made a category error.
  2. In a stable patient, hold the antibiotics and get the bone culture. IDSA 2015 supports holding empiric therapy until a microbiological diagnosis is established in the neurologically and haemodynamically stable patient. A 48-hour delay costs nothing in a six-week disease; a negative culture costs you the whole course.
  3. Never treat a sinus-tract or wound swab. It grows colonising flora, not the bone pathogen. Culture bone.
  4. Oral is non-inferior to IV. OVIVA (NEJM 2019, n=1054) settled this. What bone infection needs is a bioavailable drug, a susceptible organism, source control and a reliable patient — not a PICC line. Every line you avoid is a line infection you avoid.
  5. Six weeks, counted from the last debridement. Not from admission, not from the first dose. And if all the infected bone was resected — a clean-margin toe amputation — the answer is 2–5 days, not six weeks (IWGDF/IDSA 2023, Table 5). This single point is the most commonly over-treated scenario in medicine.
  6. Longer is not safer — except in prosthetic joint infection. Tone (Diabetes Care 2015) tripled the GI adverse-event rate going from 6 to 12 weeks and gained nothing. But DATIPO (NEJM 2021) is the counterexample that keeps you honest: in PJI, 6 weeks was not non-inferior to 12, and failure roughly doubled (18.1% vs 9.4%). Short courses are right almost everywhere in this disease — and wrong in an infected prosthesis.
  7. Absence of fever and a normal white count mean nothing. Fever is absent in about half of vertebral osteomyelitis and most diabetic-foot disease; the WBC is usually normal. The findings that are reliable are focal pain and a raised ESR/CRP.
  8. Trend the CRP, not the ESR. CRP has a ~19-hour half-life; ESR takes weeks to fall and will still be high in a patient doing perfectly well. IDSA 2015: markers that are flat or rising at ~4 weeks should raise suspicion of failure — but persistently raised markers alone, in a patient who is clinically better, do not signify failure.
  9. Treat the patient, not the picture. IDSA 2015 explicitly advises against operating on a patient whose bony imaging looks worse at 4–6 weeks but who is clinically improving with falling markers. Bone imaging lags healing badly.
  10. MSSA on vancomycin is a medication error. Cefazolin or nafcillin outperform vancomycin for MSSA. Switch the moment the sensitivity lands.
  11. Rifampin: never alone, never early. It is the only agent that reliably kills staphylococci inside biofilm (Zimmerli, JAMA 1998 — 100% vs 58% cure with implants) — but resistance emerges within days as monotherapy. Add it only after the bacteraemia has cleared, only with a companion drug, and only when staph is confirmed. And remember it is a CYP inducer that will silently defeat warfarin, DOACs, the OCP, tacrolimus and methadone.
  12. Probe-to-bone is free and it works. Sensitivity ~87%, specificity ~83% in the diabetic foot. Do it at every visit — but only trust your own result if you have been trained in the technique.
  13. The ABI lies in diabetes and CKD. Medial arterial calcification makes the vessels non-compressible, so the ABI comes back normal or >1.3 in a foot with no perfusion. Use toe pressures or TcPO₂. And remember that in an ischaemic foot, revascularisation is antimicrobial therapy.
  14. Back pain + fever + a new neurological deficit = epidural abscess until MRI says otherwise — and the full triad is present in only a minority, so do not wait for it. Emergent whole-spine MRI (skip lesions are real) and a neurosurgical decision the same hour. Recovery is a direct function of how long the cord has been compressed.
  15. Persistent S. aureus bacteraemia beyond 72 hours of appropriate therapy means an undrained focus. Not a resistant organism, not a dosing problem — a collection you have not found. Get the echo, re-image, and call the surgeon.
If you remember nothing else: find the bug, drain the pus, cut out the dead bone, then treat for six weeks starting from the day the surgeon last finished — and choose the route that gets the patient home fastest.

Refs

Sources & guidelines

🧪

Landmark trials — what they showed and why they matter

TrialYearDesignResultWhy it matters
OVIVA
Li HK et al., NEJM		 2019 Open-label, non-inferiority RCT. n=1054, 26 UK centres. Oral vs IV antibiotics for the first 6 weeks of therapy for bone & joint infection. Definitive treatment failure at 1 year: risk difference −1.38% (90% CI −4.94 to +2.19) → oral NON-INFERIOR to IV. Also saved £2,740 per patient with no difference in QALYs. The single most practice-changing trial in this disease. Destroyed the dogma that bone infection requires six weeks of IV therapy. Justifies early oral step-down with a bioavailable agent → fewer lines, fewer line infections, earlier discharge, lower cost.
Bernard et al.
The Lancet		 2015 Open-label, non-inferiority RCT. n=359, 71 French centres. 6 vs 12 weeks of antibiotics for microbiologically confirmed pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis. Cure at 1 year: 90.9% (6 wk) vs 90.8% (12 wk) → non-inferior. Established 6 weeks as the standard duration for native vertebral osteomyelitis and underpins IDSA 2015 Recommendation 26. Twelve weeks buys toxicity, not cure.
DATIPO
Bernard A et al., NEJM
THE COUNTEREXAMPLE		 2021 Multicentre, open-label, non-inferiority RCT. n=410. 6 vs 12 weeks of antibiotics for microbiologically confirmed prosthetic joint infection managed with standard surgery. Persistent infection: 18.1% (35/193) with 6 weeks vs 9.4% (18/191) with 12 weeks. Non-inferiority was NOT shown — the short course produced roughly double the failure rate. The essential brake on the "shorter is always better" message. Every other trial on this page supports shortening — DATIPO says prosthetic joint infection is the exception. Do not generalise OVIVA/Bernard 2015 durations to a PJI. This is an easy and consequential error.
Zimmerli et al.
Foreign-Body Infection (FBI) Study Group, JAMA		 1998 RCT in staphylococcal orthopaedic implant infection. After 2 weeks IV, randomised to ciprofloxacin + rifampin vs ciprofloxacin + placebo. Small (33 enrolled; 24 evaluable) and stopped early. Cure 100% (12/12) with rifampin vs 58% (7/12) without (p=0.02, as-treated). The foundation of rifampin combination therapy for biofilm/implant infection. Small and imperfect (cipro monotherapy in the control arm is now considered suboptimal), but it is why we add rifampin to staphylococcal hardware infections at all.
Tone et al.
Diabetes Care		 2015 Multicentre open-label RCT. n=40. 6 vs 12 weeks of antibiotics for non-surgically treated diabetic foot osteomyelitis. Remission similar: 60% (6 wk) vs 70% (12 wk), p=0.50. But GI adverse events: 15% vs 45% (p=0.04). Supports 6 weeks — not 12 — for medically managed DFO, and demonstrates concretely that a longer course buys harm, not cure. Cited by IWGDF/IDSA 2023.
Gariani et al.
Clin Infect Dis		 2021 Prospective, randomised, non-inferiority pilot trial. n=93. 3 vs 6 weeks of antibiotics for DFO after surgical debridement. Remission 84% (3 wk) vs 73% (6 wk), p=0.21 — comparable, with comparable adverse events. Supports the 3-week course after debridement with a positive bone margin in IWGDF/IDSA 2023. Reinforces the central principle: duration is set by how much infected bone was left behind.
Lázaro-Martínez et al.
Diabetes Care		 2014 RCT comparing antibiotics alone vs conservative surgery for diabetic foot osteomyelitis without ischaemia or necrotising infection. Comparable healing rates and time to healing between medical and surgical arms. Established that selected diabetic foot osteomyelitis — non-ischaemic, no necrotising infection, no exposed bone — can be cured with antibiotics alone. Not every DFO needs an operation; the art is picking which ones.
